subtopics.title: Velocity, acceleration and components
subtopics.theory_md:
Differentiate a vector function component by component: $\vec r=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$ gives $\dfrac{d\vec r}{dt}=\dot x\hat i+\dot y\hat j+\dot z\hat k$.

- Velocity $\vec v=\dfrac{d\vec r}{dt}$, speed $|\vec v|$, acceleration $\vec a=\dfrac{d^2\vec r}{dt^2}$.
- **Component along** $\vec b$ is $\vec v\cdot\hat b=\dfrac{\vec v\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|}$ (divide by $|\vec b|$).
- Unit tangent $\hat T=\dfrac{d\vec r/dt}{|d\vec r/dt|}$.

Differentiate first, then put in the value of $t$.
subtopics.basics_md: A moving particle has a position at each instant. How fast the position changes is the velocity; how fast the velocity changes is the acceleration. Each of $x,y,z$ is differentiated on its own.
key_points: Differentiate each component separately, then substitute $t$
$\vec v=d\vec r/dt$, $\vec a=d^2\vec r/dt^2$, speed is $|\vec v|$
Component along $\vec b$: dot with the unit vector $\vec b/|\vec b|$

questions.q: For $\vec r=t^2\hat i+t\hat j$, the velocity at $t=1$ is
questions.why: $\vec v=2t\hat i+\hat j$, which is $2\hat i+\hat j$ at $t=1$.

questions.q: The component of $\vec v$ along $\vec b$ is
questions.why: Dot with the unit vector $\hat b$, so divide by $|\vec b|$.

questions.q: A particle moves along $\vec r=e^{-t}\hat i+2\cos3t\,\hat j+2\sin3t\,\hat k$. Find the magnitudes of its velocity and acceleration at $t=0$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\vec v=-e^{-t}\hat i-6\sin3t\,\hat j+6\cos3t\,\hat k$; at $t=0$: $\vec v=-\hat i+6\hat k$, so $|\vec v|=\sqrt{1+36}=\sqrt{37}$.

$\vec a=e^{-t}\hat i-18\cos3t\,\hat j-18\sin3t\,\hat k$; at $t=0$: $\vec a=\hat i-18\hat j$, so $|\vec a|=\sqrt{1+324}=\sqrt{325}=5\sqrt{13}$.
points: $\vec v$ found by differentiating each component

questions.q: A particle moves along $x=2t^2$, $y=t^2-4t$, $z=3t-5$. Find the components of its velocity and acceleration at $t=1$ in the direction $\hat i-3\hat j+2\hat k$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\vec v=4t\hat i+(2t-4)\hat j+3\hat k$; at $t=1$: $\vec v=4\hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k$.
$\vec a=4\hat i+2\hat j$.

Unit vector: $\hat b=\dfrac{\hat i-3\hat j+2\hat k}{\sqrt{14}}$.

Component of velocity $=\dfrac{4+6+6}{\sqrt{14}}=\dfrac{16}{\sqrt{14}}=\dfrac{8\sqrt{14}}{7}$.
Component of acceleration $=\dfrac{4-6+0}{\sqrt{14}}=-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{14}}=-\dfrac{\sqrt{14}}{7}$.

questions.q: Find the unit tangent vector to the curve $x=t^2+1$, $y=4t-3$, $z=2t^2-6t$ at $t=2$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\dfrac{d\vec r}{dt}=2t\hat i+4\hat j+(4t-6)\hat k$; at $t=2$: $4\hat i+4\hat j+2\hat k$, magnitude $\sqrt{16+16+4}=6$.

$\hat T=\dfrac{4\hat i+4\hat j+2\hat k}{6}=\dfrac{2\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k}{3}$.
points: $d\vec r/dt$ at $t=2$ is $4\hat i+4\hat j+2\hat k$

subtopics.title: Product rules and constant magnitude
subtopics.theory_md:
Product rules look like ordinary calculus, but **keep the order in a cross product**:
$$\frac{d}{dt}(\vec A\cdot\vec B)=\vec A'\cdot\vec B+\vec A\cdot\vec B',\qquad \frac{d}{dt}(\vec A\times\vec B)=\vec A'\times\vec B+\vec A\times\vec B'.$$

- Constant magnitude: differentiate $\vec r\cdot\vec r=c^2$ to get $\vec r\cdot\vec r'=0$, so $\vec r\perp\vec r'$.
- $\vec r'\times\vec r'=\vec 0$, so $\dfrac{d}{dt}(\vec r\times\vec r')=\vec r\times\vec r''$.
- Constant direction means $\vec r\times\vec r'=\vec 0$.
subtopics.basics_md: A vector that only turns, never stretches, moves at right angles to itself: think of a stone on a string. That is why $\vec r\cdot\vec r'=0$.
key_points: Dot and cross product rules mirror ordinary product rule
Order in the cross product must be kept
$\vec r'\times\vec r'=\vec 0$ is the step that simplifies

questions.q: If $\vec r(t)$ has constant magnitude, then
questions.why: Differentiate $\vec r\cdot\vec r=c^2$: $2\vec r\cdot\vec r'=0$. The cross-product option is the constant-direction condition.

questions.q: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\vec r\times\dfrac{d\vec r}{dt}\right)=\vec r\times\dfrac{d^2\vec r}{dt^2}$.
questions.model_answer_md:
By the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(\vec r\times\vec r')=\vec r'\times\vec r'+\vec r\times\vec r''$.
Since a vector crossed with itself is $\vec 0$, this equals $\vec r\times\vec r''$.
points: Product rule for cross product with order kept

questions.q: If $\vec r=\vec a\cos\omega t+\vec b\sin\omega t$, where $\vec a,\vec b$ are constant vectors, show that $\vec r\times\dfrac{d\vec r}{dt}=\omega\,\vec a\times\vec b$ and $\dfrac{d^2\vec r}{dt^2}=-\omega^2\vec r$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\vec r'=\omega(-\vec a\sin\omega t+\vec b\cos\omega t)$.

$\vec r\times\vec r'=\omega\left[\cos^2\omega t\,(\vec a\times\vec b)-\sin^2\omega t\,(\vec b\times\vec a)\right]$, using $\vec a\times\vec a=\vec b\times\vec b=\vec 0$.
Since $\vec b\times\vec a=-\vec a\times\vec b$, this is $\omega(\cos^2\omega t+\sin^2\omega t)\,\vec a\times\vec b=\omega\,\vec a\times\vec b$.

$\vec r''=-\omega^2(\vec a\cos\omega t+\vec b\sin\omega t)=-\omega^2\vec r$.
points: Self cross products vanish and $\vec b\times\vec a=-\vec a\times\vec b$

questions.q: $\dfrac{d}{dt}(\vec A\times\vec B)$ equals
questions.why: Product rule with the order $\vec A$ then $\vec B$ kept in each term; option 2 swaps the second term.

subtopics.title: Gradient and the normal to a surface
subtopics.theory_md:
$\nabla=\hat i\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}+\hat j\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}+\hat k\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}$, so $\nabla\phi=\phi_x\hat i+\phi_y\hat j+\phi_z\hat k$ (a vector from a scalar).

$\nabla\phi$ is **normal to the level surface** $\phi=c$. So:
- unit normal $\hat n=\dfrac{\nabla\phi}{|\nabla\phi|}$ at the point;
- tangent plane at $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$: $\nabla\phi\cdot(\vec r-\vec r_0)=0$.

Write the surface as $\phi(x,y,z)=0$ first, then substitute the point.
subtopics.basics_md: A surface $\phi=c$ is a contour of the scalar $\phi$. The gradient points in the direction in which $\phi$ rises fastest, which is straight off the surface, so it is the normal.
key_points: Unit normal is $\nabla\phi/|\nabla\phi|$ at the point

questions.q: The vector normal to the surface $\phi(x,y,z)=c$ is
questions.why: The gradient is perpendicular to level surfaces.

questions.q: Find the unit normal and the tangent plane to the surface $z=x^2+y^2$ at the point $(1,2,5)$.
questions.model_answer_md:
Take $\phi=x^2+y^2-z$. Then $\nabla\phi=2x\hat i+2y\hat j-\hat k$, which at $(1,2,5)$ is $2\hat i+4\hat j-\hat k$ with $|\nabla\phi|=\sqrt{21}$.

Unit normal: $\hat n=\dfrac{2\hat i+4\hat j-\hat k}{\sqrt{21}}$.

Tangent plane: $2(x-1)+4(y-2)-(z-5)=0$, that is $2x+4y-z=5$.

questions.q: Find $\nabla\phi$ at $(1,-2,-1)$ for $\phi=3x^2y-y^3z^2$.

subtopics.title: Angle between two surfaces
subtopics.theory_md:
The angle between two surfaces at a common point is the angle between their **normals**:
$$\cos	heta= rac{
abla\phi_1\cdot
abla\phi_2}{|
abla\phi_1|\,|
abla\phi_2|}.$$

- First check the point lies on both surfaces.
- The surfaces cut **orthogonally** when $
abla\phi_1\cdot
abla\phi_2=0$.
- Write each surface as $\phi=0$ before taking the gradient.
subtopics.basics_md: Two surfaces meet along a curve. At a point of it, each has a flat tangent plane, and the angle between the planes is the angle between their normals.
key_points: Angle between surfaces is the angle between normals
Orthogonal when the dot product is zero
Verify the point satisfies both surfaces

questions.q: Two surfaces cut orthogonally at a point when
questions.why: Orthogonal surfaces have perpendicular normals. The cross product being zero means the surfaces touch.

questions.q: Find the angle between the surfaces $x^2+y^2+z^2=9$ and $z=x^2+y^2-3$ at the point $(2,-1,2)$.
questions.model_answer_md:
Check: $4+1+4=9$ and $4+1-3=2$, so the point lies on both.

$\phi_1=x^2+y^2+z^2-9$: $\nabla\phi_1=(2x,2y,2z)=(4,-2,4)$, $|\nabla\phi_1|=6$.
$\phi_2=x^2+y^2-z-3$: $\nabla\phi_2=(2x,2y,-1)=(4,-2,-1)$, $|\nabla\phi_2|=\sqrt{21}$.

$\nabla\phi_1\cdot\nabla\phi_2=16+4-4=16$.

$\cos\theta=\dfrac{16}{6\sqrt{21}}=\dfrac{8}{3\sqrt{21}}$, so $\theta=\cos^{-1}\dfrac{8}{3\sqrt{21}}\approx 54.4^\circ$.

questions.q: Find the constant $a$ so that the surfaces $ax^2-yz=(a+2)x$ and $4x^2y+z^3=4$ cut orthogonally at $(1,-1,2)$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\phi_1=ax^2-yz-(a+2)x$: $\nabla\phi_1=(2ax-(a+2),\,-z,\,-y)$, at the point $(a-2,\,-2,\,1)$.
$\phi_2=4x^2y+z^3-4$: $\nabla\phi_2=(8xy,\,4x^2,\,3z^2)$, at the point $(-8,\,4,\,12)$.

Orthogonal: $-8(a-2)-8+12=0\Rightarrow 20-8a=0\Rightarrow a=\dfrac52$.

subtopics.title: Gradient of functions of r
subtopics.theory_md:
With $r=|\vec r|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$, $\dfrac{\partial r}{\partial x}=\dfrac{x}{r}$, so $
abla r=\dfrac{\vec r}{r}=\hat r$.

- $
abla f(r)=f'(r)\,\dfrac{\vec r}{r}$
- $
abla r^n=n\,r^{n-2}\,\vec r$, so $
abla\dfrac1r=-\dfrac{\vec r}{r^3}$
- $
abla(\vec a\cdot\vec r)=\vec a$ for a constant vector $\vec a$.
subtopics.basics_md: $r$ is the distance from the origin; it grows fastest straight away from the origin, so its gradient is the outward unit vector.

questions.q: $\nabla\left(\dfrac1r\right)$ equals
questions.why: $n=-1$ in $nr^{n-2}\vec r$ gives $-r^{-3}\vec r$.

questions.q: Prove that $\nabla r^n=n\,r^{n-2}\,\vec r$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}r^n=nr^{n-1}\dfrac{\partial r}{\partial x}=nr^{n-1}\dfrac{x}{r}=nr^{n-2}x$, and similarly for $y,z$.

So $\nabla r^n=nr^{n-2}(x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k)=nr^{n-2}\vec r$.

questions.q: If $\vec a$ is a constant vector, show that $\nabla(\vec a\cdot\vec r)=\vec a$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\vec a\cdot\vec r=a_1x+a_2y+a_3z$.

$\nabla(\vec a\cdot\vec r)=a_1\hat i+a_2\hat j+a_3\hat k=\vec a$.

subtopics.title: Directional derivative at a point
subtopics.theory_md:
The rate of change of $\phi$ at a point along a unit vector $\hat u$ is
$$D_{\hat u}\phi=\nabla\phi\cdot\hat u.$$

1. Find $\nabla\phi$ and put in the point.
2. Convert the direction to a **unit** vector (a direction "towards a point $Q$" is $\overrightarrow{PQ}$).
3. Dot them.

A negative answer means $\phi$ decreases that way.
subtopics.basics_md: The gradient says how steeply $\phi$ changes in each coordinate direction. Dotting with a unit direction picks out the share of it along that direction.
key_points: Direction must be made a unit vector
Sign shows whether $\phi$ increases or decreases

questions.q: The directional derivative of $\phi$ along a unit vector $\hat u$ is
questions.why: It is the dot product of the gradient with the unit direction.

questions.q: Find the directional derivative of $\phi=x^2yz+4xz^2$ at $(1,-2,-1)$ in the direction $2\hat i-\hat j-2\hat k$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\nabla\phi=(2xyz+4z^2)\hat i+x^2z\,\hat j+(x^2y+8xz)\hat k$.
At $(1,-2,-1)$: $\nabla\phi=8\hat i-\hat j-10\hat k$.

$\hat u=\dfrac{2\hat i-\hat j-2\hat k}{3}$.

$D_{\hat u}\phi=\dfrac{16+1+20}{3}=\dfrac{37}{3}$.
points: $\nabla\phi=8\hat i-\hat j-10\hat k$ at the point

questions.q: Find the directional derivative of $\phi=x^2-y^2+2z^2$ at $P(1,2,3)$ in the direction of the line $PQ$, where $Q=(5,0,4)$. Also find its maximum rate of change at $P$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\nabla\phi=2x\hat i-2y\hat j+4z\hat k=2\hat i-4\hat j+12\hat k$ at $P$.

$\overrightarrow{PQ}=4\hat i-2\hat j+\hat k$, $|PQ|=\sqrt{21}$.

$D=\dfrac{8+8+12}{\sqrt{21}}=\dfrac{28}{\sqrt{21}}=\dfrac{4\sqrt{21}}{3}$.

Maximum rate $=|\nabla\phi|=\sqrt{4+16+144}=\sqrt{164}=2\sqrt{41}$.

questions.q: Find the directional derivative of $\phi=xy^2+yz^3$ at $(2,-1,1)$ towards the point $(1,1,2)$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\nabla\phi=y^2\hat i+(2xy+z^3)\hat j+3yz^2\hat k=\hat i-3\hat j-3\hat k$ at $(2,-1,1)$.

Direction $=(1-2,\ 1+1,\ 2-1)=(-1,2,1)$, magnitude $\sqrt6$.

$D=\dfrac{-1-6-3}{\sqrt6}=-\dfrac{10}{\sqrt6}$. The negative sign means $\phi$ decreases in that direction.

subtopics.title: Maximum rate and finding constants
subtopics.theory_md:
- $\phi$ increases fastest along $
abla\phi$, and the **maximum value of the directional derivative is $|
abla\phi|$**.
- Along $-
abla\phi$ it is $-|
abla\phi|$ (fastest decrease); along any tangent to the level surface it is $0$.
- "Maximum in a direction parallel to an axis" means $
abla\phi$ points along that axis: the other two components are $0$ and the remaining one has magnitude equal to the given maximum.

Unknown constants then come from these equations.
subtopics.basics_md: Standing on a hill, the steepest way up is the gradient direction and its steepness is $|\nabla\phi|$. Walking along a contour line, the height does not change.
key_points: Zero along directions tangent to the surface
Parallel to an axis means the other two components of $\nabla\phi$ are $0$
Use the given magnitude for the last equation

questions.q: The maximum value of the directional derivative of $\phi$ at a point is
questions.why: It equals the magnitude of the gradient, attained along the gradient.

questions.q: Find the greatest rate of increase of $\phi=x^2yz^3$ at $(2,1,-1)$ and the direction in which it occurs.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\nabla\phi=2xyz^3\,\hat i+x^2z^3\,\hat j+3x^2yz^2\,\hat k$; at $(2,1,-1)$: $-4\hat i-4\hat j+12\hat k$.

Greatest rate $=|\nabla\phi|=\sqrt{16+16+144}=\sqrt{176}=4\sqrt{11}$, along $-4\hat i-4\hat j+12\hat k$, i.e. $\dfrac{-\hat i-\hat j+3\hat k}{\sqrt{11}}$.

questions.q: Find $a,b,c$ so that the directional derivative of $\phi=axy+byz+czx$ at $(1,1,1)$ has maximum magnitude $4$ in a direction parallel to the $x$-axis (take $+\hat i$).
questions.model_answer_md:
$\nabla\phi=(ay+cz)\hat i+(ax+bz)\hat j+(by+cx)\hat k=(a+c)\hat i+(a+b)\hat j+(b+c)\hat k$ at $(1,1,1)$.

Parallel to $x$-axis: $a+b=0$ and $b+c=0$. Magnitude 4 along $+\hat i$: $a+c=4$.

So $b=-a$, $c=a$, $2a=4$: $a=2,\ b=-2,\ c=2$.
points: $\hat j,\hat k$ components set to zero
$a=6,\ b=24,\ c=-8$ (or the sign-reversed set for $-\hat k$)

topics.topic: Divergence and curl of a vector point function

subtopics.title: Divergence and curl
subtopics.theory_md:
For $\vec F=P\hat i+Q\hat j+R\hat k$:
$$\nabla\cdot\vec F=P_x+Q_y+R_z\ \ (\text{scalar}),\qquad \nabla\times\vec F=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ \partial_x&\partial_y&\partial_z\\ P&Q&R\end{vmatrix}\ \ (\text{vector}).$$

Expanded curl: $(R_y-Q_z)\hat i+(P_z-R_x)\hat j+(Q_x-P_y)\hat k$. Differentiate first, substitute the point at the end. Divergence measures net outflow per unit volume; curl measures rotation.
subtopics.basics_md: Divergence asks "is more flowing out of this point than in?" Curl asks 'does a tiny paddle wheel placed here spin?'
key_points: Curl is a vector from the determinant
Differentiate first, then substitute the point

questions.q: Divergence of a vector field is a
questions.why: $\nabla\cdot\vec F=P_x+Q_y+R_z$ is a number at each point; the curl is the vector.

questions.q: Find $\nabla\cdot\vec F$ and $\nabla\times\vec F$ at $(1,-1,1)$ for $\vec F=xy^2\hat i+2x^2yz\,\hat j-3yz^2\hat k$.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Divergence:** $\nabla\cdot\vec F=y^2+2x^2z-6yz$. At $(1,-1,1)$: $1+2+6=9$.

**Curl:**
- $\hat i$: $R_y-Q_z=-3z^2-2x^2y=-3+2=-1$
- $\hat j$: $P_z-R_x=0-0=0$
- $\hat k$: $Q_x-P_y=4xyz-2xy=-4+2=-2$

$\nabla\times\vec F=-\hat i-2\hat k$.

questions.q:
Find $
abla\cdot\vec F$ and $
abla	imes\vec F$ for $\vec F=
abla(x^3+y^3+z^3-3xyz)$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\vec F=3(x^2-yz)\hat i+3(y^2-zx)\hat j+3(z^2-xy)\hat k$.

$\nabla\cdot\vec F=6x+6y+6z=6(x+y+z)$.

Curl: $\hat i$: $R_y-Q_z=-3x+3x=0$; similarly $\hat j$ and $\hat k$ components are $0$. So $\nabla\times\vec F=\vec 0$ (the curl of a gradient is zero).
points: $\vec F$ found by taking the gradient

subtopics.title: Irrotational, solenoidal and potential
subtopics.theory_md:
- **Irrotational** (conservative): $\nabla\times\vec F=\vec 0$. Then $\vec F=\nabla f$ for a scalar potential $f$.
- **Solenoidal**: $\nabla\cdot\vec F=0$.

To find unknown constants, put the curl components (or the divergence) equal to zero. To find $f$, integrate $f_x=P$ with respect to $x$, add an unknown function $g(y,z)$, then match $f_y=Q$ and $f_z=R$.
subtopics.basics_md: Irrotational: no spinning anywhere. Solenoidal: nothing is created or destroyed, so whatever flows in flows out.
key_points: Integrate $f_x=P$, then fix the leftover function using $Q$ and $R$

questions.q: A field with $\nabla\times\vec F=\vec 0$ is called
questions.why: Zero curl is irrotational; zero divergence is solenoidal.

questions.q: Show that $\vec F=(y+z)\hat i+(z+x)\hat j+(x+y)\hat k$ is irrotational and find $f$ with $\vec F=\nabla f$.
questions.model_answer_md:
Curl: $\hat i$: $R_y-Q_z=1-1=0$; $\hat j$: $P_z-R_x=1-1=0$; $\hat k$: $Q_x-P_y=1-1=0$. So $\nabla\times\vec F=\vec 0$.

$f_x=y+z\Rightarrow f=xy+xz+g(y,z)$. $f_y=x+g_y=z+x\Rightarrow g=yz+h(z)$. $f_z=x+y+h'=x+y\Rightarrow h=C$.

$f=xy+yz+zx+C$.

questions.q: Find $a$ so that $\vec F=(x+3y)\hat i+(y-2z)\hat j+(x+az)\hat k$ is solenoidal.
questions.model_answer_md: $\nabla\cdot\vec F=1+1+a=0$, so $a=-2$.

subtopics.title: Standard identities
subtopics.theory_md:
- $
abla	imes(
abla\phi)=\vec 0$ (gradient fields are irrotational).
- $
abla\cdot(
abla	imes\vec F)=0$ (curl fields are solenoidal).
- $
abla^2\phi=
abla\cdot
abla\phi=\phi_{xx}+\phi_{yy}+\phi_{zz}$ (Laplacian).
- $
abla\cdot(r^n\vec r)=(n+3)r^n$, so it is solenoidal for $n=-3$.
- $
abla^2 r^n=n(n+1)r^{n-2}$, so $
abla^2\dfrac1r=0$.
- $
abla	imes(r^n\vec r)=\vec 0$.
subtopics.basics_md: The order of mixed partial derivatives does not matter. That single fact is why the curl of a gradient and the divergence of a curl cancel to zero.

questions.q: $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\vec F)$ equals
questions.why: It is a scalar and is always zero. Option 2 is a zero vector, which is the wrong type.

questions.q: Show that $\nabla\cdot(r^n\vec r)=(n+3)r^n$. For which $n$ is $r^n\vec r$ solenoidal?
questions.model_answer_md:
$
abla\cdot(r^n\vec r)=
abla r^n\cdot\vec r+r^n(
abla\cdot\vec r)$.
$
abla r^n=nr^{n-2}\vec r$, so the first term is $nr^{n-2}(\vec r\cdot\vec r)=nr^n$. And $
abla\cdot\vec r=3$.

Sum $=nr^n+3r^n=(n+3)r^n$. It is solenoidal when $n=-3$.

questions.q: Show that $\nabla^2 r^n=n(n+1)r^{n-2}$ and deduce $\nabla^2(1/r)=0$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$
abla^2r^n=
abla\cdot(nr^{n-2}\vec r)=n(n-2+3)r^{n-2}=n(n+1)r^{n-2}$, using $
abla\cdot(r^m\vec r)=(m+3)r^m$ with $m=n-2$.

For $n=-1$: $(-1)(0)r^{-3}=0$, so $
abla^2(1/r)=0$.

subtopics.title: Line integral and work done
subtopics.theory_md:
Work done by $\vec F$ along a curve $C$ is $\displaystyle W=\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r=\int_C(P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz)$.

1. Parametrise $C$: $x(t),y(t),z(t)$ (or $y=f(x)$).
2. Write $d\vec r=(x'\hat i+y'\hat j+z'\hat k)\,dt$ and put $\vec F$ in terms of $t$.
3. Integrate the dot product between the limits.

Reversing the direction of $C$ changes the sign. For a closed curve use $\oint$.
subtopics.basics_md: Adding up force times small displacement along the path gives work. Writing the path as a function of one variable turns it into an ordinary integral.
key_points: Limits are the parameter values at the end points

questions.q: The work done by a force $\vec F$ along a curve $C$ is
questions.why: Work is force dotted with displacement.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r$ for $\vec F=x^2\hat i+xy\,\hat j$ along $y=x^2$ from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$.
questions.model_answer_md:
On $y=x^2$: $dy=2x\,dx$.

$\vec F\cdot d\vec r=x^2\,dx+x\,y\,dy=x^2\,dx+x(x^2)(2x\,dx)=(x^2+2x^4)\,dx$.

$\displaystyle\int_0^1(x^2+2x^4)\,dx=\frac13+\frac25=\frac{11}{15}$.

questions.q: Find the work done by $\vec F=3xy\,\hat i-5z\,\hat j+10x\,\hat k$ along the curve $x=t^2+1$, $y=2t^2$, $z=t^3$ from $t=1$ to $t=2$.
points: $d\vec r$ and $\vec F$ in terms of $t$

subtopics.title: Conservative fields and path independence
subtopics.theory_md:
If $\nabla\times\vec F=\vec 0$ (in a simply connected region), $\vec F=\nabla\phi$ and the line integral is **independent of the path**:
$$\int_A^B\vec F\cdot d\vec r=\phi(B)-\phi(A),\qquad \oint_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r=0.$$

Test the curl, find the potential $\phi$ by integrating, then evaluate at the end points. No parametrisation is needed.
subtopics.basics_md: Walking up a hill, the height gained depends only on where you start and end, not on the winding path. A conservative field behaves like that.

questions.q: For a conservative field, $\oint_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r$ over a closed curve is
questions.why: Potential at the end point equals potential at the start point.

questions.q: Show that $\vec F=(2xy+z^3)\hat i+x^2\hat j+3xz^2\hat k$ is conservative. Find its potential and the work done from $(1,-2,1)$ to $(3,1,4)$.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Curl:** $R_y-Q_z=0-0$, $P_z-R_x=3z^2-3z^2=0$, $Q_x-P_y=2x-2x=0$. So $\nabla\times\vec F=\vec 0$ and $\vec F$ is conservative.

**Potential:** $\phi_x=2xy+z^3\Rightarrow\phi=x^2y+xz^3+g(y,z)$; $\phi_y=x^2$ gives $g_y=0$; $\phi_z=3xz^2$ gives $g_z=0$. So $\phi=x^2y+xz^3$.

**Work:** $W=\phi(3,1,4)-\phi(1,-2,1)=(9+192)-(-2+1)=201+1=202$ units.

questions.q: State the condition for a line integral $\int_A^B\vec F\cdot d\vec r$ to be independent of the path, and what it equals.
questions.model_answer_md: The path-independence condition is $\nabla\times\vec F=\vec 0$ (so $\vec F=\nabla\phi$). The integral then equals $\phi(B)-\phi(A)$, and is $0$ around any closed curve.
points: Value $\phi(B)-\phi(A)$, zero on a closed path

subtopics.title: Flux through a surface
subtopics.theory_md:
Flux of $\vec F$ through $S$ is $\displaystyle\iint_S\vec F\cdot\hat n\,dS$.

For a surface $\phi(x,y,z)=0$, $\hat n=\dfrac{\nabla\phi}{|\nabla\phi|}$. Project on a coordinate plane (say $xy$):
$$\iint_S\vec F\cdot\hat n\,dS=\iint_R\frac{\vec F\cdot\hat n}{|\hat n\cdot\hat k|}\,dx\,dy.$$

Put $z$ from the surface equation into $\vec F$, and take the projected region $R$ from the boundaries of $S$. For a cylinder use $x=a\cos\theta,\ y=a\sin\theta$, $dS=a\,d\theta\,dz$.
subtopics.basics_md: Flux counts how much of the field passes through a surface, like water through a net. Only the part of $\vec F$ along the normal passes through.
key_points: Limits come from the projected region

questions.q: For a surface $\phi=0$, projected on the $xy$-plane, $dS$ equals
questions.why: The tilted area is larger than its shadow by the factor $1/|\hat n\cdot\hat k|$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\iint_S\vec F\cdot\hat n\,dS$ for $\vec F=(x+y^2)\hat i-2x\hat j+2yz\,\hat k$ over the part of the plane $2x+y+2z=6$ in the first octant.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\phi=2x+y+2z-6$, $\nabla\phi=2\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$, $|\nabla\phi|=3$, $\hat n\cdot\hat k=\dfrac23$.

Projection on the $xy$-plane: triangle $0\le x\le3$, $0\le y\le6-2x$, with $z=\dfrac{6-2x-y}{2}$.

Using $\vec n'=(2,1,2)$: $\vec F\cdot\vec n'=2(x+y^2)-2x+4yz=2y^2+4yz$. With $4yz=2y(6-2x-y)$ this is $12y-4xy$.

$\vec F\cdot\hat n\,dS=\dfrac{\vec F\cdot\vec n'}{n'_z}\,dx\,dy=(6y-2xy)\,dx\,dy$.

$\displaystyle\iint=\int_0^3\int_0^{6-2x}(6y-2xy)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^3(3-x)(6-2x)^2\,dx=\int_0^3 4(3-x)^3\,dx=81.$

Flux $=81$ units.

questions.q: Evaluate $\iint_S\vec F\cdot\hat n\,dS$ for $\vec F=z\,\hat i+x\,\hat j-3y^2z\,\hat k$ over the part of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=16$ in the first octant between $z=0$ and $z=5$.
questions.model_answer_md:
On the cylinder $\hat n=\dfrac{x\hat i+y\hat j}{4}$. Take $x=4\cos\theta,\ y=4\sin\theta$, $dS=4\,d\theta\,dz$, with $0\le\theta\le\frac\pi2$, $0\le z\le5$.

$\vec F\cdot\hat n=\dfrac{zx+xy}{4}$, so $\vec F\cdot\hat n\,dS=(zx+xy)\,d\theta\,dz=(4z\cos\theta+16\sin\theta\cos\theta)\,d\theta\,dz$.

$\displaystyle\int_0^5\!\!\int_0^{\pi/2}=4\cdot\frac{25}{2}\cdot1+16\cdot\frac12\cdot5=50+40=90$ units.

subtopics.title: Scalar surface integrals and area
subtopics.theory_md:
For a scalar $f$: $\displaystyle\iint_S f\,dS=\iint_R f\,\frac{dx\,dy}{|\hat n\cdot\hat k|}$, and the area of $S$ is the case $f=1$.

- Plane $x+y+z=1$ in the first octant: $\hat n=\dfrac{(1,1,1)}{\sqrt3}$, so $dS=\sqrt3\,dx\,dy$.
- Sphere of radius $a$, upper half: $z=\sqrt{a^2-x^2-y^2}$ and $dS=\dfrac{a}{z}\,dx\,dy$.
subtopics.basics_md: A tilted patch has more area than its shadow. The factor $1/|\hat n\cdot\hat k|$ corrects the shadow back into the true area.

questions.q: The surface area of $S$ is given by
questions.why: Take $f=1$ in the scalar surface integral.

questions.q: Find the area of the part of the plane $x+y+z=1$ in the first octant.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\hat n=\dfrac{\hat i+\hat j+\hat k}{\sqrt3}$, so $\hat n\cdot\hat k=\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$ and $dS=\sqrt3\,dx\,dy$.

Projection is the triangle with area $\dfrac12$.

Area $=\sqrt3\cdot\dfrac12=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ square units.

questions.q: Evaluate $\iint_S z\,dS$ over the upper hemisphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2$, $z\ge0$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$dS=\dfrac{a}{z}\,dx\,dy$, so $z\,dS=a\,dx\,dy$.

$\displaystyle\iint_S z\,dS=a\iint_{x^2+y^2\le a^2}dx\,dy=a\cdot\pi a^2=\pi a^3$.
points: Area of disc $\pi a^2$, result $\pi a^3$

subtopics.title: Evaluating a flux by the divergence theorem
subtopics.theory_md:
For a **closed** surface $S$ enclosing volume $V$, with outward normal,
$$\iint_S\vec F\cdot\hat n\,dS=\iiint_V\nabla\cdot\vec F\,dV.$$

Use it to avoid summing over several faces: find $\nabla\cdot\vec F$, then integrate over $V$ (Cartesian for a box, cylindrical for a cylinder, find the base region first for a region between two surfaces). If $\nabla\cdot\vec F$ is a constant $k$, the answer is $k\times$ volume.
subtopics.basics_md: What leaves through the boundary equals what is created inside. Divergence is the creation rate at each point, and we add it up over the volume.
key_points: If $\nabla\cdot\vec F$ is constant, answer is constant times volume

questions.q: The divergence theorem converts a surface integral of $\vec F\cdot\hat n$ over a closed surface into
questions.why: Gauss: flux out equals the volume integral of the divergence.

questions.q: Use the divergence theorem to evaluate $\iint_S\vec F\cdot\hat n\,dS$ for $\vec F=x^3\hat i+y^3\hat j+z^3\hat k$ over the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\nabla\cdot\vec F=3x^2+3y^2+3z^2=3r^2$.

$\displaystyle\iiint_V3r^2\,dV=\int_0^a3r^2\cdot4\pi r^2\,dr=12\pi\cdot\frac{a^5}{5}=\frac{12\pi a^5}{5}$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\iint_S\vec F\cdot\hat n\,dS$ for $\vec F=4x\hat i-2y^2\hat j+z^2\hat k$ over the closed surface bounded by $x^2+y^2=4$, $z=0$, $z=3$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\nabla\cdot\vec F=4-4y+2z$.

Cylindrical: $x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta$, $0\le r\le2$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, $0\le z\le3$.

$\displaystyle\iiint(4-4y+2z)\,dV=4V-4\iiint y\,dV+2\iiint z\,dV$.
$V=\pi(2)^2(3)=12\pi$; $\iiint y\,dV=0$ by symmetry; $\iiint z\,dV=\dfrac92\cdot4\pi=18\pi$.

Flux $=48\pi-0+36\pi=84\pi$.

points: Flux equals the volume of the region

subtopics.title: Verifying the divergence theorem
subtopics.theory_md:
To **verify**, compute both sides and show they are equal.

- **Volume side:** $\iiint\nabla\cdot\vec F\,dV$.
- **Surface side:** flux through *every* face of the closed surface, each with its **outward** normal, then add. For a cube, faces $x=0$ and $x=1$ have $\hat n=\mp\hat i$, and so on. For a sphere of radius $a$, $\hat n=\vec r/a$ and $dS$ totals $4\pi a^2$.

State "both equal ..., hence verified".
subtopics.basics_md: A check that two different routes to the same quantity agree. Work out the left side, work out the right side, compare.
key_points: Evaluate the flux on every face with outward normal

questions.q: To verify the divergence theorem for a cube you must compute
options: only the flux through one face
the volume integral and the total flux through all six faces
questions.why: Verification needs both sides, and the surface side includes all faces.

questions.q: Verify the divergence theorem for $\vec F=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$ over the unit cube $0\le x,y,z\le1$.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Volume:** $\nabla\cdot\vec F=3$, so $\iiint3\,dV=3(1)=3$.

**Surface:** on $x=1$: $\vec F\cdot\hat i=1$, flux $=1$; on $x=0$: $-x=0$, flux $0$. Likewise $y=1$ gives $1$, $z=1$ gives $1$, and $y=0$, $z=0$ give $0$.

Total $=3$. Both sides equal $3$, so the theorem is verified.

questions.q: Verify the divergence theorem for $\vec F=x^2\hat i+y^2\hat j+z^2\hat k$ over the unit cube $0\le x,y,z\le1$.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Volume:** $\nabla\cdot\vec F=2(x+y+z)$, $\displaystyle\iiint=2\left(\tfrac12+\tfrac12+\tfrac12\right)=3$.

**Surface:** on $x=1$: $F_x=1$, flux $1$; on $x=0$: $0$. Same for $y$ and $z$. Total $=3$.

Both sides equal $3$: verified.
points: Three faces with flux 1, three with 0
Total $\frac32$, equal to volume side: verified

subtopics.title: Evaluating a line integral by Stokes' theorem
subtopics.theory_md:
For a closed curve $C$ bounding a surface $S$ (orientation by the right-hand rule):
$$\oint_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r=\iint_S(\nabla\times\vec F)\cdot\hat n\,dS.$$

1. Find $\nabla\times\vec F$.
2. Choose the simplest $S$ with boundary $C$ (for a triangle, the plane through it).
3. For a plane $z=f(x,y)$ with upward normal, $\hat n\,dS=(-f_x,-f_y,1)\,dx\,dy$; integrate over the projected region.
subtopics.basics_md: Adding up the tiny spins over a surface gives the circulation round its edge. The inner circulations cancel and only the boundary is left.
key_points: Stokes: $\oint\vec F\cdot d\vec r=\iint(\nabla\times\vec F)\cdot\hat n\,dS$
Pick the simplest surface on the curve
Use the projection for a plane: $\hat n\,dS=(-f_x,-f_y,1)\,dx\,dy$

questions.q: Stokes' theorem relates a line integral around $C$ to
questions.why: The surface integral of the curl. Option 4 is Green's theorem, the plane special case.

questions.q: Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate $\oint_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r$ for $\vec F=y^2\hat i+x^2\hat j-(x+z)\hat k$, where $C$ is the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0,0)$, $(1,0,0)$, $(1,1,0)$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\nabla\times\vec F=(0-0)\hat i+(0+1)\hat j+(2x-2y)\hat k=\hat j+2(x-y)\hat k$.

The triangle lies in the plane $z=0$, so $\hat n=\hat k$ and $dS=dx\,dy$; the region is $0\le y\le x\le1$.

$\displaystyle\iint2(x-y)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1\left[2xy-y^2\right]_0^x dx=\int_0^1x^2\,dx=\frac13$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\oint_C(y\,dx+z\,dy+x\,dz)$, where $C$ is the circle $x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2$, $x+y+z=0$, taken so that its normal is $\dfrac{\hat i+\hat j+\hat k}{\sqrt3}$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\vec F=y\hat i+z\hat j+x\hat k$, $\nabla\times\vec F=-\hat i-\hat j-\hat k$.

Take $S$ as the flat disc in the plane $x+y+z=0$ bounded by $C$; $\hat n=\dfrac{\hat i+\hat j+\hat k}{\sqrt3}$.

$(\nabla\times\vec F)\cdot\hat n=-\dfrac{3}{\sqrt3}=-\sqrt3$.

The plane passes through the origin, so $C$ is a great circle of radius $a$ with disc area $\pi a^2$.

$\oint_C=-\sqrt3\,\pi a^2$.
points: Flat disc as the surface, $\hat n=(1,1,1)/\sqrt3$

subtopics.title: Verifying Stokes' theorem
subtopics.theory_md:
To **verify**, evaluate both sides.

- **Line side:** parametrise the boundary $C$ (for a hemisphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2$, $z\ge0$, it is the circle $x^2+y^2=a^2$, $z=0$: $x=a\cos t,\ y=a\sin t$, anticlockwise from above) and integrate $\vec F\cdot d\vec r$.
- **Surface side:** $\nabla\times\vec F$, then $\iint(\nabla\times\vec F)\cdot\hat n\,dS$. If the curl is $c\,\hat k$, the integral is $c\times$ area of the projection on the $xy$-plane.

Show the two are equal.
subtopics.basics_md: Stokes' theorem says the answer depends only on the edge of the surface. So the hemisphere and the flat disc under it give the same number.
key_points: Boundary of the upper hemisphere is the circle in $z=0$
Line integral by parametrising the circle
Surface integral by curl and projection
State that both sides are equal

questions.q: The boundary of the surface $x^2+y^2+z^2=16$, $z\ge0$ is
questions.why: A hemisphere's edge is the circle where it meets the plane $z=0$.

questions.q: Stokes' theorem gives the same value for the hemisphere and for the flat disc under it because
options: they have the same boundary curve
questions.why: The theorem's value depends only on the boundary and the field.

questions.q: Verify Stokes' theorem for $\vec F=-y\hat i+x\hat j$ over the disc $x^2+y^2\le1$, $z=0$.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Line integral:** $x=\cos t,\ y=\sin t$: $\oint(-y\,dx+x\,dy)=\int_0^{2\pi}(\sin^2t+\cos^2t)\,dt=2\pi$.

**Surface integral:** $\nabla\times\vec F=(1+1)\hat k=2\hat k$, $\hat n=\hat k$: $\iint2\,dA=2\pi$.

Both equal $2\pi$: verified.

points: Boundary: circle $x^2+y^2=16$, $z=0$; $\vec v\cdot d\vec r=(3x-y)\,dx$ with $x=4\cos t,\ y=4\sin t$
Curl: $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ components $0$, $\mathbf k$ component $1$
Boundary circle $x^2+y^2=9$, $z=0$ anticlockwise: $x=3\cos t,\ y=3\sin t$

subtopics.title: Evaluating a line integral by Green's theorem
subtopics.theory_md:
For a closed curve $C$ in the plane, taken **anticlockwise**, bounding region $R$:
$$\oint_C(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=\iint_R\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy.$$

- Sketch $R$ from the given curves and fix limits (polar for circles and sectors).
- Work done by $\vec F=P\hat i+Q\hat j$ around $C$ is this same integral.
- **Area** $=\dfrac12\oint(x\,dy-y\,dx)$.
- Green's theorem is Stokes' theorem in the $xy$-plane.
subtopics.basics_md: Add up the small spins ($Q_x-P_y$) over the region, and what remains is the circulation round its edge.
key_points: Sketch the region and set the limits

questions.q: In Green's theorem the integrand of the double integral is
questions.why: It is the $\hat k$ component of the curl. $P_x+Q_y$ is the divergence.

questions.q: Use Green's theorem to evaluate $\oint_C(3x-8y^2)\,dx+(4y-6xy)\,dy$ where $C$ is the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$Q_x-P_y=-6y+16y=10y$.

Region: $0\le x\le1$, $0\le y\le1-x$.

$\displaystyle\iint10y\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1 5(1-x)^2\,dx=\frac53$.

questions.q: Using the area formula from Green's theorem, find the area of the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1$.
questions.model_answer_md:
Area $=\dfrac12\oint(x\,dy-y\,dx)$. With $x=a\cos t,\ y=b\sin t$: $x\,dy-y\,dx=ab(\cos^2t+\sin^2t)\,dt=ab\,dt$.

Area $=\dfrac12\int_0^{2\pi}ab\,dt=\pi ab$.

questions.q: Evaluate $\oint_C(y-\sin x)\,dx+\cos x\,dy$, where $C$ is the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(\pi/2,0)$, $(\pi/2,1)$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$P=y-\sin x$, $Q=\cos x$: $Q_x-P_y=-\sin x-1$.

Region: $0\le x\le\frac\pi2$, $0\le y\le\frac{2x}{\pi}$.

$\displaystyle\iint=\int_0^{\pi/2}(-\sin x-1)\frac{2x}{\pi}\,dx=-\frac2\pi\int_0^{\pi/2}x\sin x\,dx-\frac2\pi\cdot\frac{\pi^2}{8}$.
$\int_0^{\pi/2}x\sin x\,dx=1$.

Result $=-\dfrac2\pi-\dfrac\pi4$.

points: Curves meet at $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$; $x^2\le y\le\sqrt x$

subtopics.title: Verifying Green's theorem
subtopics.theory_md:
To verify, compute both sides and show they agree.

- **Double integral side:** $\iint_R(Q_x-P_y)\,dA$ over the region.
- **Line side:** $\oint_C$ taken **anticlockwise**, as the sum over the sides or arcs of $C$; on a side with $y$ fixed, $dy=0$, on a side with $x$ fixed, $dx=0$. A side traversed downward or leftward has its limits reversed.
subtopics.basics_md: Same idea as every verification: two different routes to one number. Take care with the direction of each side.
key_points: On a horizontal side $dy=0$; on a vertical side $dx=0$

questions.q: On a side of $C$ where $x$ is constant, which term of $\oint P\,dx+Q\,dy$ vanishes?
questions.why: $dx=0$ on a vertical side, so only $Q\,dy$ remains.

questions.q: Going round a rectangle anticlockwise, along its top side the variable $x$ goes
questions.why: Anticlockwise: right along the bottom, up the right side, left along the top, down the left side.

questions.q: Verify Green's theorem for $\oint_C(xy+y^2)\,dx+x^2\,dy$, where $C$ is bounded by $y=x$ and $y=x^2$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$P=xy+y^2$, $Q=x^2$: $Q_x-P_y=2x-(x+2y)=x-2y$.

**Double integral:** region $x^2\le y\le x$, $0\le x\le1$:
$\displaystyle\int_0^1\left[xy-y^2\right]_{x^2}^{x}dx=\int_0^1(-x^3+x^4)\,dx=-\frac14+\frac15=-\frac1{20}$.

**Line integral (anticlockwise):**
- Along $y=x^2$, $(0,0)\to(1,1)$: $\int_0^1(x^3+x^4+2x^3)\,dx=\frac34+\frac15=\frac{19}{20}$.
- Along $y=x$, $(1,1)\to(0,0)$: $\int_1^0(2x^2+x^2)\,dx=-1$.

Sum $=\frac{19}{20}-1=-\frac1{20}$. Both sides equal, so verified.

points: LHS side by side: bottom $0$, right $e^{-\pi/2}$, top $e^{-\pi/2}-1$, left $-1$
